messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 53-year-old social worker, married, who for the past eighteen months has been unable to step into an elevator without his chest tightening and his mouth going dry. That particular difficulty began after a home visit he made to a client in a basement apartment, a small, windowless room where the client, a man in his late forties, locked the door and assaulted him. The assault lasted perhaps twenty minutes, but David remembers every second of the helplessness—and the shame that followed, hot and suffocating, as he walked out onto the street and could not find words to tell anyone what had happened. He told his wife only that the visit had been “rough,” and then pushed the whole thing from his mind. But the memory did not stay pushed. When it returned, it brought with it the same terror he had felt on the floor of that room, and with the terror came a wave of shame so acute that he would find himself unable to speak for minutes afterward, as if the words had been stolen from him all over again.

Because he could not speak about the event, David began to ruminate in private—turning over, again and again, how he might get even with the client, imagining scenarios of revenge that left him feeling more agitated and less safe. He also tried to suppress the memory outright, telling himself to stop thinking about it, but the effort only made the images surface more frequently, and each recurrence deepened his shame. That shame, in turn, made him feel vulnerable and exposed, so he started checking behind him whenever he walked from his car to the office, scanning for anyone who might be following. He became hyperaware of unfamiliar places; if a colleague suggested a meeting at a coffee shop he had never visited, he would decline, certain he could not assess the danger there. Delays also became a problem. When a client arrived late for a session, David’s first thought was that something terrible had happened—a violation, an ambush—and his heart would race until the person appeared.

The more he checked and avoided, the more his mind stayed on the assault. A glance over his shoulder would remind him of the moment the client locked the door, and he would feel the terror wash back. That terror then drove him to ruminate more intensely, and the rumination fed his sense of threat, making him certain that danger lurked around every corner, that the world was a place where he could be trapped and overpowered at any moment. He became convinced that his only safety lay in strict routines: familiar routes, predictable schedules, and rooms with unobstructed exits. His wife noticed he was no longer willing to take evening walks or visit new restaurants. When she asked why, he said he just preferred to be at home, but he did not tell her about the fantasies of revenge that occupied his mind when he sat alone in the living room, or how he had begun to avoid the office elevator entirely, climbing seven flights of stairs twice a day, his knees aching.

The cycle tightened. A delay on the subway made him think a person was following him, which made him recall the locked door, which made him ruminate on how he should have fought back, which made him even more vigilant the next time he stepped outside. He started to feel that his own mind was working against him, that no matter how carefully he planned his day, the memory would ambush him during a quiet moment and leave him shaking. At work, his supervisor noted that he was turning down home visits—the core of his job—and had become evasive when asked why. David told himself he was just being cautious, but he knew, deep down, that the caution was eating his life.

What finally brought him to a therapist was a morning when he found himself unable to enter a small conference room for a team meeting. He stood in the doorway, heart pounding, and turned around. Later that day, he sat in his car and thought about the revenge fantasies that had become a daily ritual, and for the first time he admitted to himself that those fantasies were not making him feel stronger—they were making him feel watched. He came to treatment afraid that talking about the assault would only make the shame worse, and afraid that if he did not talk about it, he would lose his job, his marriage, and any sense that he still knew who he was.
